questions.q: What makes an algorithm greedy?
questions.explain: Greedy commits to local choices. That is why it is fast (no search), and also why it can be wrong: an early choice can rule out a better answer later. Many greedy algorithms start with a sort, but that is not what defines them.
options: It uses as much memory as it can to go faster
It builds the answer step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never goes back to reconsider it
It tries every possible answer and keeps the best
It always sorts its input first

questions.q: What does this greedy change-giver print for ₦2,680?
questions.explain: Two ₦1,000 notes leave ₦680; a ₦500 leaves ₦180; then ₦100, ₦50, ₦20 and ₦10 finish it: seven pieces. There is no ₦30 note, greedy never skips the ₦10 to take two ₦5s, and it takes the ₦500 before any ₦200.

questions.q: Why does largest-note-first always give the fewest pieces for naira notes and coins?
questions.explain: This is an exchange argument. Every swap of small pieces for fewer, larger ones limits what a best answer can hold below ₦1,000: at most ₦999 (500 + 200 + 200 + 50 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 2 + 2). So for ₦3,750 a best answer needs three ₦1,000 notes, like greedy, and the argument repeats on the rest. Systems where greedy is always optimal are called canonical; many sets, such as ₦500/₦400/₦100 vouchers, are not.
options: Because it tries the notes in every possible order

Because of how the values are chosen, small pieces in a best answer can never add up to a larger note (two ₦500s would become one ₦1,000, three ₦200s would become ₦500 + ₦100, and so on), so a best answer must take as many of the largest note as greedy does
Because every naira denomination is a power of 2
Greedy works for every set of denominations

questions.q: The till holds one ₦500 note and three ₦200 notes, nothing else. A customer needs ₦600. What does largest-note-first do?
questions.explain: With a limited supply the swap argument breaks, because you cannot swap for notes you do not have. Greedy commits to the ₦500 and never reconsiders, even though three ₦200 notes would work.
options: Takes the ₦500, is left with ₦100 it cannot make, and reports that change is impossible
Gives ₦500 + ₦200 and asks for ₦100 back

questions.q: What does this greedy change from a limited till print?
questions.explain: For ₦600 the ₦500 is taken first and ₦100 cannot be made. For ₦400 the ₦500 does not fit, so two ₦200s are used. For ₦900, ₦500 + ₦200 + ₦200 works. Greedy is right for two of the three amounts, which is exactly why a few manual tries can miss the bug.
options:
stuck with 100 left
stuck with 400 left
500+200+200

stuck with 100 left
200+200
stuck with 0 left

questions.q: Airtime vouchers come in ₦500, ₦400 and ₦100. For a ₦800 top-up, what do greedy and the best answer give?
questions.explain: ₦500, ₦400, ₦100 is not a canonical set: taking the biggest voucher first leaves ₦300, which needs three ₦100s.
options: Both give ₦400 + ₦400
Greedy gives ₦500 + ₦100 + ₦100 + ₦100 (4 vouchers); the best is ₦400 + ₦400 (2 vouchers)
Greedy gives ₦500 + ₦400 (too much)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ₦1,200: two ₦500s and two ₦100s, 4 vouchers (the best is three ₦400s). ₦900: ₦500 + ₦400, which happens to be optimal. ₦800 with ₦750 and ₦400: greedy takes ₦750, leaving ₦50, and gives up, although two ₦400s work.
options: 4 2 impossible
3 2 impossible

questions.q: With a ₦750 voucher in the set, greedy reports that ₦800 is impossible while ₦400 + ₦400 exists. What does this teach about greedy failures?
questions.explain: Greedy commits to ₦750 and cannot recover. Treat "greedy found nothing" as proof of nothing unless you have proved the greedy rule correct for that setting.
options: Greedy only ever fails by giving slightly too many pieces
A failing greedy algorithm can also give no answer, or a wrong "no", not just a worse answer
The ₦750 voucher is invalid
Greedy should never be used for money

questions.q: The lesson finds the fewest vouchers with a BFS over amounts. What are the vertices and edges of that graph?
questions.explain: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph, and each step here is one voucher. It is always correct, at a cost of O(amount × number of denominations).
options: Vertices are vouchers, edges connect vouchers of similar value
Vertices are amounts from ₦0 to the target; each voucher value is an edge from an amount to that amount plus the value, so the fewest steps is the fewest vouchers
Vertices are customers, edges are purchases
It is not a graph problem; BFS is used only as a loop

questions.q: To accept the most bookings in one meeting room, why is "accept the booking that starts earliest" a bad rule?
questions.explain: Starting early says nothing about how much of the day a booking uses up. One counterexample is enough to reject a greedy rule.
options: It is slower than the other rules
A long booking that starts first (say 08:00 to 18:00) is accepted and blocks every other booking of the day
It cannot handle bookings that touch
It is actually optimal

questions.q: Why is "accept the shortest booking first" wrong?
questions.explain: Shortest first often does well, which is what makes it dangerous. The brute-force test in the lesson found a counterexample after 19 random days.
options: Short bookings cannot overlap long ones
A short booking can overlap two longer bookings that could both have been accepted, for example 11:30 to 12:30 between 09:00 to 12:00 and 12:00 to 15:00
It always accepts fewer bookings than earliest start
It is correct; it is the same as earliest end

questions.q: Why is "accept the booking that ends earliest" the right greedy rule for one room?
questions.explain: That swap is the exchange argument: the earliest-ending booking ends no later than the best schedule's first booking, so it cannot create a new conflict. Repeat on what is left.
options: Because it accepts the longest bookings
The booking that ends first leaves the most time for everything after it; any best schedule can have its first booking swapped for it without losing anything
Because it processes bookings in the order they were made
Because it checks every pair of bookings

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By end time: A (12), B (13), D (14), C (15), E (16). A is accepted; B starts at 11, before 12, rejected; D starts at 13, accepted; C starts at 12, before 14, rejected; E starts at 14, accepted.
options: ADE
ACE
ABDE
BDE

questions.q: Bookings are treated as half-open intervals [start, end). Which condition says two bookings overlap?
questions.explain: With half-open intervals, a booking ending at 10:00 and one starting at 10:00 do not overlap, which is what people expect. The <= version would count them as a clash. The last option ignores the case where b ends before a starts.
options: a.start <= b.end && b.start <= a.end
a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end
a.start === b.start
a.end > b.start

questions.q: Times are minutes since midnight. What does this print?
questions.explain: Touching at either end (10:00 or 09:00) is not an overlap. One minute of shared time is. A booking entirely inside another overlaps too, which the one-sided check a.end > b.start would also say, but that check wrongly reports an overlap for a booking that ends before the standup starts.
options: false false true true
true true true true
false false true false
true false true true

questions.q: Why does the lesson convert "09:30" to 570 minutes before scheduling?
questions.explain: "9:30" < "10:00" is false because "9" comes after "1". Parse and validate at the boundary, and work with numbers inside.
options: Numbers use less memory than strings
String comparison is unreliable for times written in different ways ("9:30" sorts after "10:00"), while numbers compare correctly; converting once at the edge also validates the input
Because JavaScript cannot compare strings
To support time zones

questions.q: What is the idea of an exchange argument?
questions.explain: For one meeting room: swap the optimal schedule's first booking for greedy's earliest-ending booking; the schedule stays valid and the same size. Repeat for each later booking.
options: Compare greedy with brute force on random inputs
Show that any optimal answer can be changed step by step into the greedy answer without getting worse, so the greedy answer is optimal too
Swap the input order and check that the output does not change
Exchange the greedy rule for a better one when it fails

questions.q: "Greedy stays ahead" for the one-room problem means:
questions.explain: If greedy is never behind after each step, another schedule cannot fit a booking that greedy could not also fit, so it cannot end up with more bookings.
options: Greedy accepts bookings before other algorithms do
After k accepted bookings, greedy's k-th booking ends no later than the k-th booking of any other valid schedule, so greedy always has at least as much room left
Greedy is faster than every other algorithm
Greedy's first booking starts earliest

questions.q: At 10:45 three meetings are running at once, and that is the most at any moment of the day. What is the fewest rooms needed to host all meetings?
questions.explain: The maximum number running at once (the depth) is a lower bound. The greedy assignment only opens a new room when all existing rooms are busy, which means that many meetings are running together, so it never exceeds the depth.
options: At least 4, to be safe
Exactly 3: at least 3 because they run together, and assigning each meeting in start order to any free room never needs more than that
It depends on the order the bookings were made
As many rooms as there are meetings

questions.q: This sweep counts how many meetings run at once. What does it print?
questions.explain: Ends are processed before starts at the same hour (−1 sorts before +1), so a meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 are never counted together. At any moment at most two meetings run: for example 9-12 with 10-11, or 11-13 with 12-13. Sorting starts first would wrongly report 3.

questions.q: What does this room assignment print?
questions.explain: Sorted by start (ties by end): B, A, C, D. B takes room 1 and A room 2. C starts at 10, when room 1 is free (B ended at 10). D starts at 11, when room 2 is free (A ended at 11). Two rooms suffice.
options: B1 A2 C1 D2 2
A1 B2 C1 D2 2
B1 A2 C3 D2 3
A1 B2 C3 D1 3

questions.q: A conference centre has 300 rooms and 20,000 meetings a day. The assignment code scans all rooms with findIndex for each meeting. What is the better data structure, and the resulting cost?
questions.explain: The only question per meeting is "which room frees up earliest, and is it free yet?", which a min-heap answers at the root. Each meeting then costs O(log rooms) instead of O(rooms).
options: A hash map of rooms, O(n)
A min-heap of rooms ordered by the time they become free: O(n log n) including the sort
A sorted array of meetings, O(n²)
A trie of room names

questions.q: This merges bookings into busy periods, joining touching ones. What does it print?
questions.explain: 9-10 and 10-11 touch and merge; 10.5-12 overlaps and extends to 12. 13-13.5 lies inside 13-14, and Math.max keeps the end at 14 instead of shrinking it. 15-16 stands alone.

questions.q: A van takes 100 kg of bulk goods sold by weight (rice, beans, palm oil). Why is "load the highest value per kg first, then fill the rest with part of the next" optimal?
questions.explain: This is the fractional knapsack. The exchange works kilogram by kilogram because nothing is lumpy. Whole items break it.
options: Because bulk goods are cheap
Because goods can be split: if a load contains lower-value-per-kg goods while better ones are left, swapping a kilogram raises the value, so the best load takes the best goods first
Because the van is large enough for everything
It is not optimal; you need dynamic programming

questions.q: What does this greedy loader print for a 60 kg van?
questions.explain: Beans (₦1,800/kg) go first, all 30 kg. Rice is next: only 30 kg of room is left, so 30 of its 40 kg are taken. Garri never gets in. 30 × 1,800 + 30 × 1,400 = ₦96,000.
options: 30kg beans, 30kg rice 96000
30kg beans, 40kg rice 110000
50kg garri, 10kg beans 63000
40kg rice, 20kg beans 92000

questions.q: A 100 kg van, whole items only: a generator (60 kg, ₦420,000), a fridge (50 kg, ₦330,000) and a TV (50 kg, ₦320,000). What happens with "best value per kg first"?
questions.explain: With whole items, an early choice uses capacity in a lumpy way that blocks a better combination. The 0/1 knapsack needs an exact method such as dynamic programming.
options: It takes the fridge and the TV, the best load
It takes the generator (best per kg), then nothing else fits: ₦420,000, while fridge + TV would be ₦650,000
It takes all three
It splits the fridge to fill the van

questions.q: What is the most effective way to catch a wrong greedy rule before it reaches production?
questions.explain: Brute force is slow but obviously correct, and small inputs keep it fast. Disagreements give you a concrete counterexample. Property-testing libraries such as fast-check automate this and shrink failing inputs.
options: Try it on the example from the ticket
Review the code carefully
Compare it with a brute-force solution on many small random inputs, and print the first input where they disagree
Measure its running time

questions.q: Deliveries happen one after another. What does this print?
questions.explain: In deadline order: B finishes at 10 (deadline 15), A at 40 (deadline 40), C at 60 (deadline 90): nobody is late. In the original order, B finishes at 40, 25 minutes past its deadline of 15.
options: BAC 0 25
BAC 0 0
ABC 25 25
BAC 5 25

questions.q: To minimise the worst lateness of a rider's deliveries (done one after another), which greedy rule is optimal?
questions.explain: Swapping two neighbouring deliveries that are out of deadline order never makes the worst lateness larger, so repeatedly swapping reaches deadline order without getting worse. Riding times do not enter the rule.
options: Shortest delivery first
Longest delivery first
Earliest deadline first, regardless of how long each delivery takes
Nearest customer first

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is greedy: it always finalises the closest unfinished city. What makes that choice safe?
questions.explain: The safety of a greedy choice always rests on a property of the problem. For Dijkstra it is non-negative weights; with a negative "rebate" edge the same greedy choice can be wrong.
options: Cities are processed in alphabetical order
Road lengths are never negative, so no route through a city that is farther away can come back shorter
It uses a heap
It checks every route before finalising

questions.q: Two receptionists accept overlapping bookings for the same room at the same moment; each checked for conflicts before saving. How do you make the no-overlap rule hold?
questions.explain: Checks in application code race with each other. A database constraint is checked atomically when the row is written, no matter which code path writes it.
options: Run the greedy scheduler again every night
Check twice in the application before saving
Let the database enforce it, for example with a PostgreSQL exclusion constraint on the room and time range, so the second insert fails
Ask receptionists to refresh the page before booking

questions.q: A routing team uses a greedy rule ("always drive to the nearest undelivered address next") that is not optimal. When is that a reasonable engineering choice?
questions.explain: Many routing and packing problems have no known fast exact algorithm. Fast heuristics that are usually within a few percent of optimal are standard, as long as the objective and the trade-off are explicit.
options: Never; non-optimal algorithms are bugs
When the exact problem is too expensive to solve at the required size and speed, the greedy result is usually close enough, and everyone knows it is an approximation
Only when there are fewer than ten addresses
When the greedy rule has been proved optimal

questions.q: Write changeCounts(amount) that returns how many of each naira denomination to hand over, largest first, as a string like 1000x3 500x1 200x1 50x1 (only denominations used). It should print that for ₦3,750 and then 5x1 2x2 for ₦9.
questions.explain: Division gives the count of each note at once, instead of a loop per note: O(d) for d denominations. Amounts are whole naira, so there is no floating-point error.

questions.q: Write mostBookings(requests) that returns the names of the largest set of non-overlapping bookings (half-open intervals, times in minutes), using the earliest-end rule. It should print standup, review, lunch, retro.
questions.explain: Sort by end, then accept whatever starts when the room is free (>=, so touching bookings are fine). The workshop and the demo each block two shorter bookings.

questions.q: Write roomsNeeded(meetings) that returns the fewest rooms needed for all meetings (half-open intervals in hours), with a sweep: +1 at each start, −1 at each end, ends before starts at the same time. It should print 3 1 0.
questions.explain: At 10:30 three meetings run at once. Back-to-back meetings share one room because ends are processed first at equal times. The maximum depth is both a lower bound and achievable, so it is the answer. Sorting makes it O(n log n).

questions.q: Write busy(bookings) that merges overlapping or touching bookings (in hours) into busy periods, in start order. It should print 8-9.5 10-12 14-15.
questions.explain: After sorting by start, each booking either extends the last period (it starts at or before the period's end) or opens a new one. Math.max keeps a period from shrinking when a booking lies inside it.

questions.q: Write bestLoad(goods, capacity) for goods that can be split by weight: take the highest value per kg first, and part of the next one if it does not fit. Return the total value in naira. It should print 177000 0.
questions.explain: 30 kg at ₦2,100, 40 kg at ₦1,800 and the remaining 30 kg at ₦1,400: ₦177,000. Sorting by value per kg is the greedy choice; it is optimal only because goods can be split.

questions.q: Order the deliveries by earliest deadline first and return the worst lateness (how far past its deadline the latest delivery arrives, 0 if none are late). Deliveries run one after another from time 0. It should print CAB 5.
questions.explain: C finishes at 10 (deadline 20), A at 35 (deadline 40), B at 65 (deadline 60, so 5 minutes late). No order does better: the total riding time is 65 minutes, and the last delivery can have a deadline of at most 60.

questions.q: Greedy fails for vouchers of ₦500, ₦400 and ₦100. Write fewest(amount, values) that returns the true fewest number of vouchers, by building a table best[a] for every amount from 0 up (the fewest for a is 1 plus the fewest for a - value, over all values). Return -1 if impossible. It should print 2 3 2 -1.
questions.explain: Instead of committing to one voucher, the table tries every voucher as the last one and keeps the best, reusing answers for smaller amounts. That is dynamic programming, the subject of the lesson after next. It costs O(amount × values), far more than greedy, but it is always right.

questions.q: This compares greedy with an exact table for every amount up to 8. What does it print?
questions.explain: For 6, greedy takes 4, then 1 and 1 (3 pieces), while 3 + 3 needs only 2. Every amount below 6 happens to work. Checking all amounts up to the sum of the two largest values (here 7) is enough to decide whether a coin system is greedy-safe.
options: 6: greedy 3, best 2
5: greedy 2, best 2
7: greedy 2, best 2
null

questions.q: Two greedy rules on the same bookings (in hours). What does this print?
questions.explain: By start time the all-day 8-18 booking is accepted first and blocks everything else. By end time, 9-10, 10-11, 11-12 and 13-14 are accepted and the all-day booking is rejected.
